summary: This informational RFC discusses IPv6 Neighbor Discovery problems arising from huge /64 subnets. Simple implementations can suffer denial of service when scans create large numbers of cache entries. It describes issues and mitigations.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router cannot find a neighbor's link-layer address, it starts Neighbor Discovery and waits for a reply. A scan of many unused IPv6 addresses can overwhelm that process and disrupt other traffic.

questions: why can ipv6 neighbor discovery be attacked
how to protect a router from ndp exhaustion
what is the problem with ipv6 /64 subnets
subtitle: Why scanning large IPv6 subnets can overload Neighbor Discovery on routers.

tldr.problem: A router may try to resolve many unused IPv6 addresses when traffic scans a large subnet, consuming the resources Neighbor Discovery needs for real traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how unresolved destinations enter a queue for the Neighbor Discovery Process and gives operational mitigations and implementation priorities.
tldr.outcome: Operators receive workarounds with trade-offs, and implementors are advised to manage resources and prioritize essential Neighbor Discovery work.

today: RFC 6583 is an Informational document published in March 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it discusses operational and implementation issues in IPv6 Neighbor Discovery.

sections.title: How Address Scans Can Cause Disruption
sections.content:
IPv6 commonly uses /64 subnets, which contain many addresses that are not assigned to hosts. When a scan sends traffic toward unused addresses on a directly connected network, a router may try to resolve each destination. The scan may be intentional or may come from a legitimate inventory or security tool.

Each unresolved destination can create an incomplete Neighbor Cache entry and work for the Neighbor Discovery Process. A large number of requests can consume processing capacity and memory, replace useful mappings, and prevent new connections or disrupt existing traffic. The RFC notes that rate-limiting Neighbor Solicitations can help but does not fully solve the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: A scan of many unused IPv6 addresses can make a router spend its resources looking for neighbors that do not exist. That can leave too little capacity to find real neighbors or maintain active connections.

sections.title: What the Router Does for an Unknown Neighbor
sections.content:
A router needs a link-layer address to send a packet to a neighbor on an attached link. The forwarding plane checks the Neighbor Cache. If it has no complete entry, it queues the request and signals the Neighbor Discovery Process in the control plane.

The Neighbor Discovery Process creates an INCOMPLETE entry, sends one or more Neighbor Solicitations, and waits for a Neighbor Advertisement. A reply completes the entry and lets the router send the queued packet. If many requests fill shared queues, they can compete with address checks and maintenance for neighbors already in use.
sections.plainLanguage: The router checks a table for each neighbor's link-layer address. If an address is missing, a slower control process asks the neighbor and holds the packet until it gets a reply.

sections.title: Mitigations for Network Operators
sections.content:
The RFC describes four operational approaches and warns that some are awkward to manage. Operators can filter unused address space when hosts use static or stateful addressing, size subnets to match actual use where autoconfiguration is not needed, or route a subnet to a discard interface while hosts advertise more-specific routes.

Operators can also tune the rate at which unknown addresses enter Neighbor Discovery queues. A lower rate reduces processing load but can slow legitimate address resolution, especially after a cache reset. The RFC says this approach is worth investigating when unknown-address resolution and maintenance of existing entries use separate queues.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can limit which addresses reach a router, use smaller subnets in suitable settings, or route known hosts more specifically. Slowing address resolution can also reduce load, but it may delay legitimate traffic.

sections.title: Implementation Priorities
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that implementors manage processing and memory explicitly. When resources are limited, responding to Neighbor Solicitations for the router's own addresses and revalidating existing in-use entries should take priority over creating entries for unknown destinations.

It places requests for traffic sourced by the router above requests for unknown addresses, which should receive the lowest priority. If requests share one queue, vendors should let operators tune its rate and size, with optional per-interface or per-prefix limits. These settings require balancing resource use against the time needed to learn valid neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Router software should protect work that keeps active neighbors reachable. Requests about addresses never seen before should not crowd out replies and checks for existing connections.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC presents the problem as a denial-of-service risk that can be triggered by an attacker or by network scanning. Its mitigations aim to protect availability while vendors improve implementations.

The document cautions that implementation changes can have unforeseen consequences. It says the authors do not believe the proposed mitigations or finer-grained queues create additional security risks or denial-of-service exposure.
sections.plainLanguage: The issue can interrupt service even when a scan is not malicious. The RFC says its mitigations are not believed to add security risks, while acknowledging that implementation changes can have unexpected effects.
